transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-03-14 14:05 PT — Duration: ~73m
Attendees: Maya Chen, Oliver Grant (Redwood) — Dr. Lina Ortega, Marcus Lee, Priya Nambiar, Aaron Patel (Spectral Health)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to define POC guardrails: how many reserved GPUs we need, how the opt-in burst pool / hedging will work, fallback strategies on capacity failures, and the benchmark & timeline for a 4-week pilot. Customer emphasized patient-data residency and on-prem adjacency for a subset of workloads.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria (latency, throughput, cost per inference, quality regressions allowed)
- Workload shape and sizing (token distribution, concurrency, peak patterns)
- Reserved capacity vs opt-in burst vs shared pool hedging model
- Fallbacks: queueing, degrade to smaller model, async webhooks, partial results
- Benchmarks: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, kv cache hit-rates, failure injection tests
- Timeline & next steps for 2-week baseline + 4-week pilot

Action items recap: (see metadata list)

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, account lead, and with me is Oliver our deep tech SE.
[00:00:08] Dr. Lina Ortega: Thanks, Maya. We are trying to scope a pilot to validate that we can route production triage workloads through Redwood with predictable latency and cost, and also to make sure we don't regress clinical quality.
[00:00:22] Maya Chen: Totally. Two immediate questions from our side: what does "predictable" mean for you numerically? And can you describe the worst-case peak you expect?
[00:00:33] Marcus Lee: Great question. For the triage microservice, p95 latency under 250ms is ideal, 400ms is upper bound. Throughput: baseline 20 req/s sustained, but we see spikes up to 120 concurrent sessions over 10-15 minutes during morning batch ingest. Token sizes are variable — average 1.2k tokens, tail up to 7k.
[00:00:58] Oliver Grant: Thanks Marcus. That token tail matters a lot for GPU memory and kv caching. If you have many long sequences we'd recommend pinning a small reserved pool of GPUs for steady-state, plus an autoscale hedge that can tap into a burst pool.
[00:01:12] Priya Nambiar: When you say "hedge" can you describe the control plane? Who pays for the burst? We need clear cost boundaries.
[00:01:20] Maya Chen: Good point. Typical POC model: customer commits to N reserved GPUs (e.g., 2x H100-equivalent) for baseline throughput. Burst can be either metered from our shared pool with burst billing or configured as reserved on your side but only used during the POC. We'll include both price options in the sheet. For hedging behavior, we can do a prioritized routing policy: reserved capacity first, then opt-in burst, then degraded model fallback.
[00:01:46] Dr. Lina Ortega: Degraded model fallback — you mean reduce to a smaller model with higher hallucination risk? That's risky for clinical triage.
[00:01:53] Oliver Grant: Yes, and that's why we recommend multi-pronged fallbacks: 1) queue and return a 202 with estimated wait, 2) route to a fast condensed model that only extracts structured triage codes (less free-text), 3) if neither acceptable, fall back to a synchronous human-in-the-loop queue. We can simulate tradeoffs in the bench.
[00:02:15] Aaron Patel: Our compliance needs audit logs for every inference — model id, version, input hash — can Redwood provide immutable logs for the pilot? Also KMS integration is must-have.
[00:02:25] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We can surface audit logs and integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll provide a SOC2 + L2 security pack and also a short guide for setting up a customer-managed key.
[00:02:36] Marcus Lee: Quick nit: we will likely want the private deployment variant (VPC peered) for the pilot because PHI crosses our payloads, but initial benchmarks can run on Redwood Dedicated if we anonymize traces.
[00:02:47] Oliver Grant: That's a common path. For the POC run we recommend a two-stage approach: (A) run a 48–72 hour synthetic benchmark on Dedicated to validate latency/cost assumptions, then (B) a constrained VPC peered run with real traces for quality/regression tests. The VPC run will validate networking and KMS.
[00:03:05] Dr. Lina Ortega: What's the suggested reserved GPU sizing?
[00:03:09] Oliver Grant: Based on the traffic you gave earlier, a conservative starting point is 2x H100-ish instances for baseline — that'll give you steady throughput for small-medium token lengths. For the 7k token tails we recommend either long-sequence-optimized kernels or staging those long jobs into a queued async path. The burst pool should be able to add 4–6 additional devices to handle spikes. We'll include GPU type tradeoffs: H100 vs A100 vs an optimized L4-like setup (if quantized).
[00:03:41] Priya Nambiar: Can you explain the billing model for burst in plain terms?
[00:03:45] Maya Chen: Sure. Option A: you reserve N devices and pay monthly for them; during spikes we allocate additional on-demand burst and bill per-minute for those extra devices. Option B: you pre-commit to slightly more reserved capacity for a lower unit price and keep bursts lower. Option C: we run burst on a shared pool with a blended burst surcharge. We'll send a spreadsheet with example scenarios.
[00:04:05] Marcus Lee: On the fallback queueing — if we queue a request we still need to guarantee an SLA for time to completion, otherwise downstream teams will complain. Can Redwood expose queue depth metrics and per-request ETA?
[00:04:16] Oliver Grant: Yes. Our runtime exposes queue metrics, per-request ETA based on current token backlog, and can trigger auto-escalation rules when ETA > threshold. We can instrument request headers so your downstream services can surface ETA to users.
[00:04:30] Dr. Lina Ortega: Regarding quality — how do we guard against model drift/regressions during the POC?
[00:04:35] Maya Chen: Two parts: (1) we run eval suites against a held-out set of triage prompts to measure precision/recall or other clinical metrics at every model version, (2) we will pin model versions for the POC and only roll forward with a canary test and a small holdout. We can also set automatic rollback on quality regressions.
[00:04:53] Aaron Patel: For benchmarking, what metrics should we capture?
[00:04:56] Oliver Grant: Capture p50/p95/p99 latency per token, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, warm vs cold kernel times, memory swap events, and cost per 1k tokens. Also capture model output quality metrics defined by your clinical evals. We'll provide a benchmark template.
[00:05:10] Marcus Lee: We'll need to simulate the morning spike pattern — a 12–15 minute surge. How do you recommend shaping the load?
[00:05:17] Oliver Grant: Use a ramp-and-hold pattern with pebble spikes embedded. For the POC, we recommend two profiles: steady-state 20 req/s for 24h, and an orchestrated spike: ramp to 120 concurrent over 60s, hold 10 minutes, then ramp down. We'll run that profile multiple times to check autoscale behavior.
[00:05:34] Maya Chen: Also important: KV cache warm-up. If many requests are similar prefixes, the cache will dramatically reduce token costs. We should run a warm-up run then measure the post-warm hit-rate.
[00:05:45] Dr. Lina Ortega: On timelines, what's realistic for us to get through bench -> pilot -> decision?
[00:05:50] Maya Chen: If we start next week: 1) config & trace handoff (week 1), 2) 48–72h synthetic bench + analysis (end of week 1), 3) VPC peered constrained run with real traces + quality evals (week 2–3), 4) pilot wrap & decision meeting week 4. So roughly 3–4 weeks to decision.
[00:06:07] Priya Nambiar: What about failure injection tests? We want to see graceful degradation if a whole AZ goes down or if GPUs become overloaded.
[00:06:14] Oliver Grant: We'll include chaos tests: simulated node loss, network latency injection, and overloaded-kernel stalls. We'll observe routing policy reactions: fallback to burst, degrade model, or queue, depending on policy. We'll run these during the dedicated bench so it doesn't affect production.
[00:06:30] Marcus Lee: Are there known mis-transcriptions or naming issues we should watch for? We sometimes see "KV cash" in your docs instead of KV cache — small thing but it's confusing.
[00:06:37] Maya Chen: Haha yes our auto transcripts are messy. We'll make sure the runbook uses consistent terms.
[00:06:42] Dr. Lina Ortega: For the audit logs, what retention and format? We need 1 year retention and CSV/JSON lines output to our S3 bucket.
[00:06:50] Maya Chen: We can export logs in JSON lines to your S3 and retain at least 12 months for the pilot. We'll include sample schema.
[00:06:58] Aaron Patel: If we need an on-prem package later, is Redwood able to support air-gapped deployments for the clinical models?
[00:07:04] Oliver Grant: Yes — Redwood Private supports on-prem containers and a customer-managed control plane. That is usually a separate engagement post-POC but we can include an architecture sketch in the SOW.
[00:07:12] Marcus Lee: One operational question — how do you handle model KV cache persistence on pod restarts?
[00:07:18] Oliver Grant: The runtime preserves KV cache across warm restart in the same allocation; for hard pod eviction the cache is lost and we fall back to cold-start performance. We'll instrument restart events and include retries in the client SDK.
[00:07:30] Dr. Lina Ortega: Any quick red flags from you? Anything that would make this POC not feasible?
[00:07:33] Oliver Grant: Not from a tech perspective; just the compliance gating. If we can't get peered VPC or anonymized traces, we won't be able to validate the exact quality metrics. Also extremely long tail tokens at high concurrency will push memory needs up; we may need to shard or stream results.
[00:07:48] Maya Chen: Ok let's summarize next steps — Maya will send pricing and SOW v0; Oliver will send the benchmark runner and checklist; Marcus and team will send traces and open network/firewall; schedule the 2-hour benchmark run week of 3/22.
[00:07:58] Priya Nambiar: Sounds good. One last ask — can you include an example of a degraded-model output vs full-model output so we can assess clinical risk?
[00:08:05] Oliver Grant: Yes, we'll include a short sample set and the eval rubric.
[00:08:10] Dr. Lina Ortega: Thanks all.
[00:08:12] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the attachments.

End of transcript.
